Israel and Judah--</hi>the restoration not merely of the Jews (treated of in this thirtieth chapter), but also of the ten tribes ("Israel"; treated in the thirty-first chapter), together forming the whole nation (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.18">Jr 30:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jr 32:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.25">Eze 39:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Am 9:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">15</reference>). "Israel" is mentioned first because its exile was longer than that of Judah. Some captives of the Israelite ten tribes returned with those of Judah (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Lu 2:36</reference>; "Aser" is mentioned). But these are only a pledge of the full restoration hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>, "All Israel"). Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jr 16:15</reference>. This third verse is a brief statement of the subject before the prophecy itself is given. <div eID="gen18236" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10232"/><div sID="gen18237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10232"/><hi type="bold">5. We have heard ... trembling--</hi>God introduces the Jews speaking that which they will be reduced to at last in spite of their stubbornness. Threat and promise are combined: the former briefly; namely, the misery of the Jews in the Babylonian captivity down to their "trembling" and "fear" arising from the approach of the Medo-Persian army of Cyrus against Babylon; the promise is more fully dwelt on; namely, their "trembling" will issue in a deliverance as speedy as is the transition from a woman's labor pangs to her joy at giving birth to a child (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.6">Jr 30:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18237" type="x-p"/>

Ask--</hi>Consult all the authorities, men or books, you can, you will not find an instance. Yet in that coming day men will be seen with their hands pressed on their loins, as women do to repress their pangs. God will drive men through pain to gestures more fitting a woman than a man (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.31">Jr 4:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.24">6:24</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10234"/><div sID="gen18240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10234"/><hi type="bold">7. great--</hi>marked by great calamities (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.11">Joe 2:11</reference>, 31; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Am 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.14">Zep 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen18240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none like it ... but he shall be saved--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Da 12:1</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10235"/><div sID="gen18242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10235"/><hi type="bold">8. his yoke ... thy neck--</hi>his, that is, Jacob's (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.7">Jr 30:7</reference>), the yoke imposed on him. The transition to the second person is frequent, God speaking of Jacob or Israel, at the same time addressing him directly. So "him" rightly follows; "foreigners shall no more make him their servant" (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">Jr 25:14</reference>). After the deliverance by Cyrus, Persia, Alexander, Antiochus, and Rome made Judah their servant. The full of deliverance meant must, therefore, be still future. <div eID="gen18242" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10236"/><div sID="gen18243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10236"/>9. Instead of serving strangers (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.8">Jr 30:8</reference>), they shall serve the Lord, their rightful King in the theocracy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>).<div eID="gen18243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David, their king--</hi>No king of David's seed has held the scepter since the captivity; for Zerubbabel, though of David's line, never claimed the title of "king." The Son of David, Messiah, must therefore be meant; so the Targum (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25-Rom.11.32">Ro 11:25-32</reference>). He was appointed to the throne of David (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>). He is here joined with Jehovah as claiming equal allegiance. God is our "King," only when we are subject to Christ; God rules us not immediately, but through His Son (<reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, 23, 27).<div eID="gen18244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raise up--</hi>applied to the judges whom God raised up as deliverers of Israel out of the hand of its oppressors (<reference osisRef="Judg.2.16">Jud 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9">3:9</reference>). So Christ was raised up as the antitypical Deliverer (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.69">Lu 1:69</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>; 13:23). <div eID="gen18245" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 9. Instead of serving strangers ( Jr 30:8 ), they shall serve the Lord, their rightful King in the theocracy ( Eze 21:27 ). The Son of David, Messiah, must therefore be meant; so the Targum (compare Is 55:3 , 4 ; Eze 34:23 , 24 ; 37:24 ; Ho 3:5 ; Ro 11:25-32 ). He was appointed to the throne of David ( Is 9:7 ; Lu 1:32 ). He is here joined with Jehovah as claiming equal allegiance. God is our "King," only when we are subject to Christ; God rules us not immediately, but through His Son ( Joh 5:22 , 23, 27). raise up-- applied to the judges whom God raised up as deliverers of Israel out of the hand of its oppressors ( Jud 2:16 ; 3:9 ). So Christ was raised up as the antitypical Deliverer ( Psa 2:6 ; Lu 1:69 ; Ac 2:30 ; 13:23).

Therefore--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Jer.30.13">Jr 30:13</reference>, because "There is none to plead thy cause ... therefore" I will plead thy cause, and heal thy wound, by overwhelming thy foes. Hyrcanus (hereditary high priest and governor), only as types of Christ (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.5">Ro 9:5</reference>), the antitypical "David" (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause him to draw near--</hi>as the great Priest (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.22">Ex 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.21.17">Le 21:17</reference>), through whom believers also have access to God (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.22">He 10:19-22</reference>). His priestly and kingly characters are similarly combined (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>).<div eID="gen18276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who ... engaged ... heart to approach--</hi>literally, "pledged his heart," that is, his life; a thing unique; Messiah alone has made His life responsible as the surety (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">He 7:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11-Heb.9.15">9:11-15</reference>), in order to gain access not only for Himself, but for us to God. Heart is here used for life, to express the courage which it needed to undertake such a tremendous suretyship. The question implies admiration at one being found competent by His twofold nature, as God and man, for the task. Compare the interrogation (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.3">Is 63:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen18277" type="x-p"/>
